subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Forgetting Curve
description: A fast breakdown of The Forgetting Curve for builders.

hook.text: Within one hour, you lose over half of what you just learned. By tomorrow, it's nearly seventy percent gone.

buildup.text: Ebbinghaus plotted this in 1885 by memorizing nonsense syllables and testing himself over days.

discovery.text: Forgetting is steepest right after learning, then gradually levels off. The curve is exponential.

twist.text: Meaningful material decays slower than nonsense, but the curve's shape holds for all types of memory.

climax.text: Each review resets the curve, flattening it further. Three well-timed reviews can make memory last years.

punchline.text: Forgetting is fast. Reviewing is faster.

quiz.question: What did Ebbinghaus discover about forgetting?
options: Most forgetting happens shortly after learning

details.summary: Ebbinghaus discovered that memory decays exponentially after learning, with the steepest drop in the first hour. Without review, roughly half of new material is forgotten within a day. The forgetting curve demonstrates that memory is not permanent and that timely review dramatically slows the loss.
details.whyItMatters: The forgetting curve is the foundation of all effective study strategies. Understanding how fast we forget explains why cramming fails and spaced practice works.
takeaways: Memory decays exponentially, fastest in the first hour
About half of new material is lost within a day without review
Each review session flattens the curve and extends retention

faq.question: How did Ebbinghaus discover the forgetting curve?
faq.answer: Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and tested his recall at various intervals. He meticulously tracked how many relearning trials he needed over time. His self-experimentation in the 1880s produced the first quantitative law of memory, showing exponential decay.

faq.question: Can the forgetting curve be overcome?
faq.answer: Not eliminated but dramatically flattened. Each well-timed review strengthens the memory trace and slows subsequent decay. Spaced repetition systems exploit this by scheduling reviews just before expected forgetting. Meaningful material is also forgotten much more slowly than nonsense.
